## What is published

OPDI starts from the position reports that aircraft broadcast by ADS-B,
received by the [OpenSky Network](https://opensky-network.org/), a network of
ground receivers run by volunteers, universities and other organisations. OPDI
groups the reports of one aircraft into flights and describes each flight in
two ways.

- The **flight list** has one row per flight, also for flights for which no
  departure or destination airport could be named: the aircraft, call sign,
  departure and destination airports, first and last time seen, and main
  times, such as take-off and landing, and the runways used.
- The **flight events** have one row per event. An **event** is a moment in a
  flight with a time and a position, for example the take-off, the top of
  climb, the crossing of a flight level or the entry into a holding pattern.
  Each row also carries the **measurements** taken at that event, for example
  the distance flown since the start of the flight.

Columns are listed on the [Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd); how each is
computed is explained in [OPDI Algorithms](../algorithms/index.qmd).

## Daily files

The data is published in daily files:

| File | One row per | Size of one day |
|---|---|---|
| `flight_list/flight_list_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | flight | about 15 MB |
| `flight_events/flight_events_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | event | about 220 MB |

`YYYYMMDD` is the date, for example `20260614`. A day holds about
160,000 flights and 6.7 million events worldwide.

The files are in **Parquet**, a format that stores data by column and that most
tools read: Python (pandas, pyarrow, polars), R (arrow), DuckDB, Spark and
Trino. A program that reads only some columns or rows reads only part of the
file.

Two small files help to find data (columns on the
[Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd#flight-index-and-catalogue)):

- A **flight index** per month, `index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet`: one row
  per flight of the month and the name of the daily file that holds it.
- A **catalogue**, `catalogue.parquet`: one row per published day, with the
  number of flights and events, the time of the first and last event, the file
  sizes and the versions of the methods used.

## Which day a flight belongs to

A flight belongs to the day on which it was **first seen**, in UTC: the column
`dof` (date of flight). The files of a day hold the flights first seen that
day and **all** their events, also those after midnight: a flight that takes
off at 23:30 UTC and lands at 02:00 UTC the next day is in the files of the
day it took off, with its landing. A track that holds several flights (a
landing, then a take-off at least five minutes later) has one row for each
flight, all in the files of the day on which the track was first seen (see
[Tracks and flight identity](../algorithms/tracks.qmd#flights-of-a-track)).

## Coverage

The data cover the whole world: every flight that the OpenSky Network received.
Reception depends on where receivers are and is thin over the oceans and near
the ground at many airports; see [Limitations](../limitations.qmd#ads-b-reception).
